extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers learning basic kinematics/physics (undergraduate level or interested lay readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Explain and classify motion using geometric idealizations (point-motion, rigid-body rotation, strain), represent position relative to an origin and frame, add displacements geometrically, and plot position changes versus time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point-motion idealization
rubrics_metrics.description: Represent an extremely small object by a geometrical point moving along a geometrical curve: 'till in conception the wire ends in a geometrical line or curve, and the bead in a geometrical point.' The motion of the ideal point along the ideal curve will represent with a great degree of accuracy the motion of an extremely small button up a tube.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use successive perceptual-to-conceptual limits (man → button → bead → geometrical point) to drop perceptual elements and obtain an ideal motion that is easier to describe. Harnessing the point to the button (and the button to the man) lets point-motion describe much of the real motion (start/stop, speed, times between landings). Antipattern: relying on point-motion to capture rotations, internal limb movements, somersaults, or other 'eccentricities'—point-motion cannot tell how a rigid body has turned about the point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish translation and rotation
rubrics_metrics.description: Two fundamentally different types of motion are distinguished: motion of translation (change of position) and motion of rotation (change of aspect of a rigid body). 'The first type of motion, corresponding to change of position, is termed motion of translation; the second type, corresponding to the change of aspect of a rigid body, is termed motion of rotation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point-motion describes translation but must be supplemented to describe rotation; even for a rigid body the point-motion alone is insufficient—one must also describe how the body is facing or rotating at each instant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of rigid body (conceptual ideal)
rubrics_metrics.description: A body is said to remain rigid during any given motion when the distances between all pairs of its points remain unaltered throughout the whole duration of the motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat rigidity as a conceptual/geometrical ideal used for classification and description. Recognize that real perceptual bodies usually change form and that rigidity is a limit/convenient ideal rather than a perceptual reality. Example: a wooden chair is better approximated by the rigid-body ideal than a man, but still may deform; physicists often must treat bodies as elastic rather than rigid to describe internal mechanical action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rotation specification requires more than one point (or an axis)
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine change of aspect of a rigid body we must give the new positions of two definite points A and B of the rigid body (or equivalently specify rotation about a line through the fixed point).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stating the new position of one line (CA → CA') is insufficient to fix the body's aspect; specifying two noncollinear points (or their directions) fixes orientation. Geometrical proof: turning two lines into new positions can be effected by rotation about a certain line CO; thus rotation is described geometrically via an axis and angle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strain: change of form (stretch and slide)
rubrics_metrics.description: Strain (change of form) has two fundamental aspects: change of size without change of shape (stretch) and change of shape without change of size (slide/shearing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure stretch by the ratio of the change in length to original length (stretch) and measure dilatation (change of volume) which for small stretches ≈ three times the stretch of a diameter. Measure slide/shear by the tangent of the angle change or by the ratio of transverse displacement to reference length. Examples: blowing up a thin rubber ball (stretch/dilatation); shearing a woven fabric (slide). Emphasize that these measures presuppose geometric/conceptual constructs (diameters, straight lines, angles) absent in direct perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: All changes of form analysable into stretches and slides
rubrics_metrics.description: All changes of form whatever can be analysed into stretches and slides, or into changes of length and changes of angle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use conceptual geometrical networks (points, lines, angles) to reduce arbitrary deformations into combinations of stretches (length changes) and slides (angular/shearing changes). Reference: elementary discussions in dynamics and kinematics for formal treatments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three divisions of kinematics
rubrics_metrics.description: Kinematics (the geometry of motion) is divided into three great types: (a) the motion of a point, (b) the motion of a rigid body about a fixed point, (c) the relative motion of the parts of a body (strain).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each division uses geometrical, idealized concepts (points, lines, angles) to describe and classify perceptions of motion. These ideal modes are instruments for description and economy of thought, not explanations of phenomena themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relativity of position and motion; need for origin and frame
rubrics_metrics.description: Position of a point is relative; to represent the position of a point P we must measure it with regard to some other point O (an 'origin of reference') and specify direction and sense (bearing). 'Absolute position in space... is meaningless.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To fix a point fully you need distance from origin and bearing (direction + sense), which in three dimensions requires a frame of reference (three non-collinear standards). Choose a convenient origin/frame (e.g., sun vs earth) to simplify description; the preferred frame is the one that best economises description, not an absolute truth. Antipattern: speaking of absolute motion without specifying reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation by a directed step (vector-like step)
rubrics_metrics.description: Represent the position of P relative to O by a directed step OP: a line whose length gives magnitude, whose direction gives bearing, and with an arrow-head to mark sense. 'Such a line ... is termed a step.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A step tells how to shift from one origin to the point; steps can be composed (see parallelogram law). Note that in conceptual 3D space three standard points are needed to fix directions. Emphasize conceptual nature: steps are geometric symbols to record magnitude, direction and sense of position/displacement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parallelogram law for addition of steps (geometrical addition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Addition of displacements/steps is given by completing the parallelogram on two steps; the diagonal measures the single step equivalent to the sum of the two. 'Complete the parallelogram on two steps, and its diagonal will measure a single step equivalent to the sum of the other two.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat addition of displacements, velocities, spins, and accelerations geometrically (vector addition) rather than arithmetically; beware confusion with scalar/arithmetic addition (example: 8 + 12 = 10 'absurd' only to the arithmetician when steps are non-collinear). This is a fundamental principle used throughout kinematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time-chart / plotting position against time
rubrics_metrics.description: To study how position changes with time, plot positions at instants on a time-chart (turn into geometry a column of Bradshaw): place stations at vertical distances proportional to their real separations and plot times to visualize changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a time-chart where spatial locations are scaled along one axis and time down the other (or vice versa) so that changes of position (P6 → P7) are represented by steps whose geometric differences measure displacement per time interval (precursor to velocity). Choose appropriate scales so plotted distances reflect real distances (e.g., furlongs per inch) allowing derived quantities like parliamentary fares or speeds to be inferred. This is a graphical method to measure and visualise how displacements vary with time.
